On 4 November, sixty years after the flood, Florence woke up under a low grey sky, like the one in 1966. It wasn't raining, but the air was damp and the Arno, seen from the bridges, looked darker than usual. Graziella was already in the kitchen at six in the morning. She couldn't sleep. She said that every year, on 4 November, the smell of mud came back to her, even though sixty years had now passed. "The nose has more memory than the head," she told Pietro, who had come down for breakfast. "The head forgets. The nose doesn't."

There were commemorations all over the city. At nine the mayor laid a wreath on the Ponte Vecchio. At ten, in Piazza Santa Croce, the fire brigade sounded their sirens for a minute, at the same time as in 1966 the water had reached its highest level. On walls all over the city, next to the old plaques marking how high the river had risen, someone had stuck sheets of paper overnight with a single sentence: "We remember." Mancini, in the Gazzetta, had titled his front-page article "Sixty years on, the mud has become memory".

Mid-morning Graziella took Pietro and Viola out in front of the trattoria, onto the pavement of Via Maggio. On the wall next to the door, two and a half metres above the ground, there was a small marble plaque that nobody looked at any more, blackened by time: "The Arno reached here on 4 November 1966". Graziella pointed at it. "Up to there," she said. "I was twelve and I was this tall." She put her hand at the height of Pietro's shoulder. Viola looked up at the plaque, then at her grandmother, then at the plaque again, and asked if that was a notch too, like the ones on the little room's door frame. Graziella thought for a moment. "Yes," she replied. "It's the city's notch. It shows how high the pain was. And it helps you remember that, with time, you grow taller."

The launch of Bellini's book was set for six in the evening, in the church of San Frediano, right in front of the altar where the little Madonna had stood in 1966. It had been the confraternity prior's idea; he said there was no more fitting place. The parish priest agreed on one condition: that at the end there would also be a prayer for everyone who had lost something in 1966. Bellini accepted at once. "My grandfather would have wanted it that way," he said. "He always said restoration and prayer are alike: both are done on your knees, patiently, without knowing whether they'll work."

All afternoon the family worked to get the church ready. Matei and Marco set up a small wooden stage. Chiara and Doina, who had come back from Sibiu specially for the occasion with Ion, hung two large photographs from 1966 on either side of the altar, enlarged from the Gazzetta's archive: one showed Via Maggio buried in mud, the other a group of young people with shovels in front of Santa Croce. Davide, looking closely at the second photo, suddenly stopped and called his mother. In the middle of the group, third from the left, was his grandfather, with the same shovel as in the family photo.

Rita looked at the photograph for a long time. Then she took out her phone and called someone. Half an hour later a tall seventy-nine-year-old man with white hair and a stick came into the church, accompanied by a small smiling lady. It was Efisio, Davide's grandfather, who had come from Sardinia in 1966 with a shovel and never left. The lady was Lucia, the San Frediano girl he had stayed for. Efisio stopped in front of the photo, recognised himself and burst out laughing. "Look at my hair," he said to Davide. "And look at that shovel. I kept it for twenty years. Then your grandmother threw it away."

Davide, who had never heard his grandfather talk about 1966 like that, asked him how he had met his grandmother. Efisio laughed and looked at Lucia. "On the third day," he said, "I was shovelling in front of a haberdasher's in Via dei Serragli. She came out with a broom, looked me up and down and said: 'You shovel badly. This is how it's done.' She took the shovel out of my hands and showed me." Lucia nodded, not in the least sorry. "He shovelled terribly," she confirmed. "I didn't manage to teach him properly before it was lunchtime. So I invited him to eat. Then he came back the next day for another lesson. With time he learned to shovel. But by then it was too late to leave."

In the meantime, the church was starting to fill. At half past five there were still thirty chairs missing, and Pietro was panicking. The prior saved the situation, arriving with ten brothers carrying the confraternity's chairs on their shoulders, the way you carry a statue in a procession. At ten to six the chairs had run out and people were standing along the aisles. Everyone was there: the neighbourhood, the family, Mancini with his recorder, Councillor Neri, Valeria Conti, Rocco the foreman, Lorenzo, Signor Franco with his paddle. And there were dozens of elderly people nobody knew, who had come alone, each with a flower in hand.

They were the mud angels. They had read Mancini's article and the news of the launch, and from all over Italy, some even from Germany and England, they had decided to come back. One had come from Turin by train, alone, at eighty-two. An English lady had brought an old diary from 1966, written in English, with the names of the churches where she had worked. A retired professor, the same one who years earlier had attended Giulia's lecture at the university, sat in the front row and recognised Bellini. "I was here, in this church," he told him. "I saw your grandfather and a young man with a red bicycle. I never managed to ask him his name."

At six sharp Bellini went up onto the stage, leaning on his stick. The church fell silent. Bellini looked at the crowd, then at the photographs from 1966, then at the empty altar where the Madonna had once stood. For a long moment he said nothing, and Pietro, in the front row, was afraid he wouldn't manage. Then Bellini opened the book at the first page and began to read, his voice a little hoarse: "It had been raining for three days. It was 3 November 1966, and Florence was going to sleep like every evening, not knowing it would not wake up in the same city…"

He read for twenty minutes. He read about the night the water rose, the two-year-old grandson asking why the street had become a river, the Madonna covered in mud, the young man with the red bicycle. As he read, the church grew quieter and quieter. The mud angels listened with their eyes closed, some moving their lips, as if they recognised the words. The English lady was crying unashamedly. Efisio, Davide's grandfather, held Lucia's hand and nodded every now and then, as if to say: it's true, that's exactly how it was.

Then Bellini closed the book and looked at Graziella, sitting in the second row with Viola in her arms. "The best chapter in this book," he said, "I didn't write. Graziella, will you read it?" Graziella went red. She hadn't expected anything of the kind. She shook her head, then looked at Pietro, who gave her an encouraging nod, then looked at the photo of Via Maggio buried in mud. She stood up. She handed Viola to Giulia, went up onto the stage with slightly trembling legs, took the book from Bellini's hands and opened it at the chapter "The Loaf".

"Once upon a time there was a twelve-year-old girl who was hungry," she read. Her voice, uncertain at first, grew steadily firmer. She read about the trattoria step, her father shovelling, her mother crying. She read about the tall young man on the red bicycle who stopped, opened his rucksack and broke the bread in two. When she reached the sentence "It was the best bread she had ever eaten", she stopped. She couldn't go on. In the silence of the church, from the back, an old woman's voice said loudly: "Me too! I got half a loaf from a young man that year too!"

Everyone turned round. Then another voice, a man's, from another part of the church: "I gave it out! I was one of those young men! We had bread from the Red Cross and we shared it with the children!" And then another, and another. Within minutes the church filled with voices remembering: who had given the bread, who had received it, who had shovelled next to whom. People who hadn't seen each other for sixty years recognised one another among the pews, stood up, embraced. Mancini, at the back of the church, had stopped recording. There was no need. Nobody who was there would ever forget it.

Graziella stayed on the stage, the book in her hand, watching the scene. Then she closed the book without finishing the chapter and said a single thing into the microphone, her voice breaking: "There. You already know the rest. You wrote it." She came down from the stage amid applause that lasted five minutes, the longest the church of San Frediano had heard in centuries. The priest, who was supposed to say the final prayer, decided that by now there was no need for words. He had the bells rung. Outside, over the Arno, evening was falling.

Later, in the sacristy, Matei discovered that the launch had been streamed live on the Gazzetta's website, and that in Valletta, in the house with the green gallarija, Camilleri, Marija and Lina had watched it all on the computer. Lina sent Giulia a message: "All three of us cried. Marija says that in 1966 the fishermen of Malta raised money for Florence. Her father was one of them." And below, a photo: Viola's cloth bunny, sitting on the windowsill of the gallarija, with the sea behind it. "I'm keeping it safe," Lina wrote. "I'll bring it at Christmas. In the meantime, it's watching the harbour for her." Giulia showed the photo to Viola, who looked at it seriously and said: "Grazzi."

After the launch, the party moved to the trattoria, of course. Graziella had made ribollita for a hundred people, "as they come, case by case", and twice as many came. The mud angels ate sitting everywhere: at the tables, on the steps, on the pavement of Via Maggio, bowls in hand. Efisio told Pietro how he had slept for three weeks in a church with forty other young men. The English lady gave Bellini her diary, "because by now it's more yours than mine". And the old man from Turin, before leaving on the last train, asked Graziella for the recipe. Graziella, for the first time in her life, gave it to him.

"Grandma!" protested Pietro when the man had gone. "You didn't even give the recipe to the mayor!" Graziella wiped her hands on her apron. "The mayor didn't shovel the mud in front of my door," she replied. "That gentleman did. I remember. He had a green woollen hat, and he brought me a bucket of clean water. I never managed to thank him, in '66." She paused. "Now I have. Sixty years late. But better late than never."

Around midnight, when the last guests had gone, the family stayed in the trattoria clearing up. Bellini was sitting at his table, tired but happy, with the English lady's diary open in front of him. Pietro sat down next to him. "Professor," he said, "today I understood something about time." "Let's hear it," said Bellini. "Time doesn't erase things," said Pietro. "It just puts them aside. Like the tin box in the attic. Then one day someone opens the box, and the things are still there, whole, waiting."

Bellini looked at him for a long time. Then he took the black notebook, the last of his diaries, and gave it to him. "You keep it," he said. "From now on you write it. I've written enough for one lifetime." Pietro looked at the notebook, then at Bellini. "But I'm not a restorer," he said. "Not yet," replied Bellini. "But you know how to look, and you know how to tell a story. With time, you learn the rest." Pietro opened the notebook at the first blank page. He wrote the date, 4 November. Then, below, in his neatest handwriting, he wrote the first line of his diary.

"Today, sixty years later, the mud came back into the church. But this time it was made of memories, and nobody needed a shovel." He read it again and thought it was fine. He showed it to Bellini, who nodded without saying anything. He showed it to his grandmother, who read it with her glasses on the tip of her nose and said only: "Well done. But also write that the ribollita ran out at ten, and that at midnight people were still asking for seconds." Pietro laughed and wrote it. Because a diary, he had learned that year, has to hold everything: the big things and the small ones. With time, you discover they're the same thing.

That night, before going to bed, Graziella stopped in front of the kitchen shelf. The tin box with the thirteen letters. The blue brush. The photo of Aldo with the red bicycle. The photo of Viorica in front of the oven. And now, next to them, Bellini's book, with Davide's cover: the Madonna lifted by two hands above a sea of mud, and the red bicycle in the corner. Graziella touched it with her fingertips. "Did you see, Aldo?" she said softly. "Sixty years. Time flies. But we still remember." Then she switched off the light and went up the stairs, one at a time, calmly.
